text: Triggers exist on all four platforms, firing before or after insert, update, or delete. The syntax differences are real, but there's one conceptual fork here that matters far more than any keyword — whether a trigger fires once per statement, or once per row. Get this wrong and your trigger logic behaves completely differently than you expect.

T-SQL's triggers are covered in depth elsewhere in this catalog, but here's the key fact for comparison. Create trigger, on production dot product, after update, as, begin, insert into price change log, select from inserted i join deleted d on i dot product id equals d dot product id, end. Inserted and deleted are virtual tables that can hold many rows at once — a single update touching five hundred rows fires this trigger exactly once, with all five hundred old-new pairs sitting right there together.

Oracle works completely differently by default. Create or replace trigger, after update on products, for each row, begin, insert into price change log values colon old dot product id, colon old dot list price, colon new dot list price, end. Colon new and colon old are single-row record references, and for each row means that same five hundred row update fires this trigger five hundred separate times — once per row, each time with a fresh colon new and colon old. T-SQL thinks in sets by default; Oracle thinks in rows.

MySQL follows Oracle's row-level approach but drops the colon. Create trigger, after update on products, for each row, begin, insert into price change log values old dot product id, old dot list price, new dot list price, end. Same one-row-at-a-time model as Oracle, just new and old with no punctuation in front.

PostgreSQL is structurally different from all three of the others. A Postgres trigger is always two separate pieces: first, a trigger function written in PL slash pgsql that holds the actual logic and references new and old with no colon, just like MySQL — and second, a create trigger statement that does nothing but name when to fire and which function to call. T-SQL, Oracle, and MySQL all put the logic directly inside create trigger. PostgreSQL never does.

Remember this one clearly: set-based versus row-level is the real split, not just syntax. T-SQL fires once per statement; Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL all fire once per row. And PostgreSQL alone splits the trigger into a function plus a trigger declaration. Last lesson of this chapter next: dynamic SQL, and a security point that matters on every single platform — never concatenate user input directly into SQL text. See you there.
